title: Episode 1 (lines 214–479)

teacherSummary.text: Oedipus curses the unknown killer and anyone who shelters him, even himself. The blind prophet Teiresias arrives but refuses to speak. Provoked, he names Oedipus as the polluter of the land and hints at worse. Oedipus accuses him and Creon of plotting to take the throne.

context.history: Teiresias is the traditional blind seer of Theban myth. In Greek belief, a killer carried pollution (miasma) that could harm a whole city.

significance: The blind man sees and the seeing man is blind. Oedipus' curse (lines 246–251) falls on himself, the play's strongest dramatic irony.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “And on the murderer this curse I lay / (On him and all the partners in his guilt):— / Wretch, may he pine in utter wretchedness!” slowly and put it in my own words: Oedipus lays a public curse on the unknown killer of Laius and on anyone who shared his guilt: may he waste away in misery. Next, craft. I notice the speech is solemn and almost legal, and the words in parentheses widen the curse to every partner in the crime. The strongest word is “wretchedness”: Oedipus will later call himself an abject wretch, so the word he aims at the killer comes back to him. Then, effect. Why is the curse Oedipus lays on the murderer dramatic irony? My answer: The curse on the murderer is dramatic irony because the audience knows that Oedipus himself is the murderer, so every misery he wishes on the killer he is laying on his own head.
